Put the lettuce, tomatoes, cucumbers, radishes, pepper, spring onions, parsley and mint in the large bowl. The salad can wait in the fridge at this point for up to an hour.

Just before serving, pour over the dressing and toss well. Add most of the toasted bread and toss once more, then scatter the remaining bread on top, sprinkle with a little more sumac and serve straight away, before the bread softens.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately; undressed vegetables keep 1 day refrigerated, and the bread keeps crisp in an airtight tin.
notes: Purslane (baqleh) is a classic addition when you can find it.

recipes.name: Baba ghanoush (smoky aubergine and tahini dip)
recipes.description: Aubergines charred until smoky and collapsing, mashed with tahini, lemon and garlic and finished with olive oil and pomegranate. Also known as mutabbal in much of the Levant.
equipment: Gas hob, barbecue or oven grill

steps.t: Prick the aubergines a few times with a fork. Set them directly on a gas flame, on a hot barbecue or under a very hot oven grill and cook, turning with tongs every few minutes, until the skin is blackened and blistered all over and the aubergines have completely collapsed: 15–20 minutes over a flame, 30–40 minutes under a grill. The charring gives the smoky flavour.

Put them in a bowl, cover with a plate and leave for 10 minutes; the steam loosens the skin. Split them open, scoop the soft flesh into the colander and discard the skin and stalks. Leave to drain for 10 minutes to get rid of the bitter juices.
Crush the garlic with the salt to a paste. Chop the aubergine flesh finely with a knife or mash it with a fork, keeping a little texture, then mix in the garlic, tahini and lemon juice.

Taste: it should be smoky, creamy and bright, so add more lemon or salt if needed. Spread on a plate, make a swirl with the back of a spoon, drizzle with olive oil and scatter with parsley and pomegranate seeds. Serve with warm pita and raw vegetables.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate covered for up to 3 days; add the garnish just before serving.

recipes.name: Kibbeh bil sanieh (baked kibbeh with pine nut filling)
recipes.description: A tray of fine bulgur and lean meat pressed in two layers around spiced lamb, onion and pine nuts, scored into diamonds and baked until crisp. Lebanon's national dish in its easiest form.
equipment: Baking tray or round tin (about 30 cm)

ingredients.name: Very lean minced beef or lamb

steps.t: Rinse the bulgur in the sieve, then cover it with cold water and soak for 15 minutes. Drain and squeeze out as much water as you can with your hands.

For the filling, heat 2 tablespoons of oil in the frying pan over medium heat and toast the pine nuts for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until golden; lift them out. Add the onions and cook for 8 minutes, until soft and golden, then add the lamb and cook on high heat for 8–10 minutes, breaking it up, until browned with no pink left. Season with the allspice, cinnamon, salt and pepper, stir in the pine nuts and leave to cool.

For the shell, pulse the grated onion with the spices and salt in the food processor. Add the lean meat and the bulgur and process in two batches, adding iced water a spoonful at a time, until it forms a smooth, sticky, dough-like paste that holds together when pressed. Knead the batches together briefly by hand.

Heat the oven to 190 °C and brush the tray with oil. Press half the shell mixture evenly over the base, about 1 cm thick, smoothing it with wet hands. Spread the cooled filling over it in an even layer.

Flatten handfuls of the remaining shell between wet palms into thin patties and lay them over the filling, overlapping slightly, then smooth and press the joins together with wet hands so the top is sealed.

Dip a sharp knife in water and score the top into diamonds, cutting through the top layer only, and run the knife around the edge. Make a small hole in the centre and drizzle the remaining oil all over so it runs into the cuts.
Bake for 35–40 minutes, until deep golden brown and crisp on top and the edges have pulled away from the tray. Rest for 10 minutes, then cut along the scored lines.
Serve warm or at room temperature with yogurt or yogurt and cucumber salad, fattoush or a simple tomato salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Shish tawook (garlic and lemon chicken skewers with toum)
recipes.description: Chicken breast marinated in yogurt, lemon, garlic and paprika, grilled on skewers until charred at the edges and served with fluffy whipped garlic sauce (toum), pickles and pita.

steps.t: Whisk the yogurt, lemon juice, olive oil, crushed garlic, tomato paste, paprika, thyme, salt and pepper in the bowl. Add the chicken, turn to coat and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, or up to 12 hours.

Make the toum: blend the garlic and salt in the food processor, scraping down the sides, until finely minced. With the motor running, pour in the oil in a very thin stream, adding the lemon juice and iced water a spoonful at a time between additions of oil. After 6–8 minutes it should be thick, white and fluffy, like mayonnaise. If it splits and turns runny, blend a fresh clove of garlic and slowly add the broken mixture back in.
Heat the grill or griddle pan until very hot. Thread the chicken onto the skewers, leaving a little space between the pieces so they cook evenly, and let excess marinade drip off.
Grill for 10–12 minutes, turning every 2–3 minutes, until charred at the edges, juicy and cooked through to 74 °C in the thickest piece. Rest for 3 minutes.
Warm the pitas on the grill for a few seconds per side.
Serve the skewers with the toum, tomatoes, lettuce, pickles and pita, or slide the chicken off into the bread with a thick smear of toum and roll it up as a sandwich.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Toum keeps for 2 weeks in a sealed jar in the fridge and is also served with roast chicken and shawarma.

recipes.name: Manakish za'atar (za'atar and olive oil flatbreads)
recipes.description: Soft, chewy flatbreads dimpled and spread with za'atar mixed with olive oil, baked very hot. Lebanon's everyday breakfast, eaten folded with tomato, cucumber, mint and olives.
equipment: Baking stone, steel or heavy baking tray

steps.t: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt in the bowl, then add the water and olive oil and bring together. Knead on a lightly floured surface for 8–10 minutes, until smooth, elastic and slightly tacky. Put it back in the oiled bowl, cover and leave somewhere warm for 1–1½ hours, until doubled.
Stir the za'atar and olive oil together into a loose, spreadable paste and leave it to soak for 10 minutes so the herbs soften.
Put the baking stone or tray on the top shelf and heat the oven to 250 °C (or its highest setting) for 30 minutes.

Divide the dough into 6 balls and rest them under a cloth for 10 minutes. Roll or press each into a round about 20 cm across and 5 mm thick, then press your fingertips all over the surface to dimple it, leaving a 1 cm rim; the dimples hold the topping in place.
Spread about 2 tablespoons of the za'atar oil over each round, right up to the rim.

Slide two at a time onto the hot stone and bake for 6–8 minutes, until the base is golden and crisp and the rim puffed and lightly browned. Watch closely at the end: za'atar darkens and turns bitter quickly.
Serve warm, folded in half or rolled around slices of tomato and cucumber, mint leaves and olives, with a glass of sweet tea.

recipes.storage: Best fresh. Wrap cooled leftovers for up to 1 day, or freeze for a month.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a hot oven or dry frying pan for 2–3 minutes.
notes: For manakish jibneh, top with grated akkawi cheese or a mix of mozzarella and feta instead of za'atar.

recipes.name: Mouhalabieh (orange blossom milk pudding)
recipes.description: A silky, delicate milk pudding thickened with cornflour and scented with orange blossom and rose water, set in small bowls and topped with ground pistachios.

ingredients.name: Honey or rose syrup, to drizzle

steps.t: Whisk the cornflour with 250 ml of the cold milk in a jug until completely smooth, with no lumps at all.

Put the rest of the milk and the sugar in the heavy saucepan over medium heat and stir until the sugar dissolves and the milk is steaming, with small bubbles around the edge, about 5 minutes. Don't let it boil over.

Whisk the cornflour mixture again and pour it into the hot milk in a steady stream, whisking constantly. Keep stirring with the spatula over medium-low heat, scraping the base and corners, for 8–10 minutes, until it thickens to a heavy custard. Once it starts to bubble slowly, cook for 2 minutes more to remove any raw starch taste.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the orange blossom water and rose water; add them gradually and taste, as brands vary in strength.
Pour into the bowls or glasses and leave to cool for 15 minutes, then cover and refrigerate for at least 3 hours, until set and cold.
Just before serving, scatter with the ground pistachios and add a thin drizzle of honey or rose syrup if you like.

recipes.storage: @chilled

recipes.name: Hummus bil lahme (hummus with spiced lamb and pine nuts)
recipes.description: Warm, freshly whipped hummus topped with sizzling minced lamb, allspice, cinnamon and toasted pine nuts in their buttery juices. A mezze favourite that makes a meal with bread and salad.

steps.t: Put the chickpeas in the saucepan, cover with fresh water and simmer for 10 minutes, until very soft; warm, soft chickpeas whip into much smoother hummus. Drain, keeping a cupful of the water, and set aside a spoonful of whole chickpeas for the garnish.

While still hot, blend the chickpeas with the garlic, lemon juice and salt for 1 minute. Add the tahini and cumin and keep blending for 3 minutes, adding the iced water a spoonful at a time (and some cooking water if needed), until pale, fluffy and very smooth. Taste for salt and lemon.

For the topping, heat the butter and oil in the frying pan over medium heat and toast the pine nuts for 2 minutes, stirring, until golden; lift them out. Add the onion and cook for 3–4 minutes until soft.

Turn the heat to high, add the lamb and cook for 6–8 minutes, breaking it up with a spoon, until browned, crisp in places and with no pink left. Season with the allspice, cinnamon, salt and pepper and stir the pine nuts back in.

Spread the hummus over two plates or a platter, making a deep well in the centre with the back of a spoon. Spoon the hot lamb and its juices into the well, then finish with the whole chickpeas, olive oil, parsley and a dusting of paprika.
Serve immediately, while the meat is sizzling and the hummus is warm, with warm pita for scooping, pickles and a chopped salad.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh; refrigerate leftover hummus and meat separately for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the lamb in a hot pan until steaming hot throughout (74 °C / 165 °F); serve the hummus at room temperature.

recipes.name: Muhammara (roasted red pepper and walnut dip)
recipes.description: Aleppo's smoky-sweet dip of charred red peppers, toasted walnuts, breadcrumbs, pomegranate molasses and Aleppo pepper, with a gentle heat. Eaten with bread or alongside grilled meat.

ingredients.name: Dry breadcrumbs (or toasted crumbs from stale bread)
Aleppo pepper (pul biber), or 1 tsp chilli flakes

steps.t: Heat the oven grill to high and grill the whole peppers close to the element, turning every few minutes, for 12–15 minutes, until blackened and blistered all over (or char them over a gas flame). Put them in a bowl, cover with a plate and leave for 10 minutes, then peel, remove the stems and seeds and pat dry.
Meanwhile, toast the walnuts in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 3–4 minutes, until fragrant, and leave to cool.

Pulse the walnuts, breadcrumbs, garlic, cumin, Aleppo pepper and salt in the food processor to coarse crumbs. Add the peppers, pepper paste, pomegranate molasses and lemon juice and pulse to a thick paste that still has some texture. With the motor running, pour in 3 tablespoons of the olive oil.

Taste and balance it: it should be sweet, sour, smoky and gently hot, so add more molasses, lemon, salt or pepper as needed. Leave for at least 30 minutes for the flavours to come together (it is even better the next day), then spread on a plate, drizzle with the rest of the oil and garnish with chopped walnuts and parsley. Serve with warm pita and raw vegetables.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate covered for up to 5 days.

recipes.name: Fatteh hummus (chickpeas and toasted bread with yogurt and pine nuts)
recipes.description: Layers of crisp toasted bread, warm cumin-scented chickpeas and garlicky yogurt-tahini sauce, crowned with pine nuts fried in butter. A Damascus Friday breakfast eaten from a shared dish.

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200 °C. Toss the torn bread with the olive oil on the baking tray and bake for 8–10 minutes, until golden and crisp. (Frying the pieces is the traditional, richer way.)
Meanwhile, put the chickpeas in the saucepan with the water, cumin and salt and simmer for 10 minutes, until very hot and soft. Keep them warm in their liquid.
Whisk the yogurt, tahini, garlic, lemon juice and salt together until smooth. The yogurt should not be fridge-cold, or the dish will be lukewarm.
Melt the butter in the small pan over medium heat and fry the pine nuts for 1–2 minutes, stirring, until golden. Take off the heat and stir in the paprika.

Assemble just before eating: spread the bread in the serving dish and spoon over a few tablespoons of the hot chickpea liquid to soften it slightly. Spoon the chickpeas over, keeping a few back, then cover with the yogurt sauce.

Pour the sizzling butter and pine nuts over the top, scatter with the reserved chickpeas, a pinch of cumin and the parsley and serve at once, while the contrast of hot and cold, crisp and soft is at its best.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately; the bread goes soggy on standing.
notes: Fatteh with chicken or aubergine is made the same way for lunch.

recipes.name: Ma'amoul (date-filled semolina cookies)
recipes.description: Tender, crumbly semolina cookies scented with orange blossom and rose water, filled with spiced date paste and pressed in carved wooden moulds. Baked for Eid and Easter across the Levant.
equipment: Ma'amoul mould (or a fork for decorating)
Baking trays lined with baking paper

steps.t: Put the semolina and flour in the bowl, pour over the melted ghee and rub it in with your fingertips for 3–4 minutes, until every grain is coated and the mixture feels like damp sand. Cover and leave at room temperature for at least 6 hours or overnight; this resting makes the cookies melt in the mouth.

Add the sugar, baking powder, orange blossom water, rose water and milk and knead briefly, just until it comes together into a soft dough that holds its shape when squeezed. Don't overwork it. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

For the filling, warm the dates with the butter and cinnamon in the small saucepan over low heat for 2–3 minutes, mashing with a fork, until they form a smooth paste. Cool, then roll into 24 balls of about 12 g each.

Heat the oven to 180 °C. Take a 30 g piece of dough, roll it into a ball and press your thumb into it, working the dough around into a thin-walled cup. Put a date ball inside and pinch the dough closed over it, then roll gently into a ball again.

Press each ball firmly into the floured mould, level the base and knock it out with a sharp tap on the work surface. Without a mould, flatten each ball slightly and decorate the top with a fork or tweezers. Arrange on the lined trays 2 cm apart.
Bake for 15–20 minutes, until the bases are golden; the tops should stay pale, which is correct. Leave to cool completely on the trays, as they are fragile while warm.
Dust with icing sugar and serve with Arabic coffee or mint tea.

recipes.storage: Keep airtight at room temperature for up to 2 weeks, or freeze for 3 months.
notes: Fill some with chopped walnuts or pistachios mixed with sugar and rose water; families use differently shaped moulds so each filling can be told apart.

recipes.name: Musakhan (sumac chicken and onions on taboon bread)
recipes.description: Roast chicken spiced with sumac and allspice, served on flatbread spread thickly with onions slowly cooked in olive oil and sumac, then baked until the bread edges crisp. Palestine's olive harvest feast.

ingredients.name: Taboon bread or other thick flatbreads (or large pitas)

steps.t: Mix the sumac, allspice, cinnamon, cardamom, salt, pepper and olive oil and rub all over the chicken pieces, getting some under the skin. Leave for 30 minutes at room temperature, or refrigerate overnight.

Heat the oven to 200 °C. Arrange the chicken skin side up in the roasting tin and roast for 45–50 minutes, until the skin is deep golden and the thickest part of a thigh reaches 74 °C with clear juices. Keep the juices in the tin.

Meanwhile, heat the 90 ml of olive oil in the large frying pan over medium-low heat. Add the onions and salt and cook gently, stirring often, for 25–30 minutes, until very soft, sweet and translucent; they should not brown. Stir in the 4 tablespoons of sumac: the onions turn a deep purple-red.
Brush the flatbreads with some of the chicken juices and oil from the roasting tin and set them on the baking trays.
Spread a thick layer of sumac onions over each bread and set the chicken pieces on top. Scatter with the toasted pine nuts and a little more sumac, and drizzle with the remaining pan juices.
Return to the oven for 8–10 minutes, until the edges of the bread are crisp and the chicken is sizzling.
Serve hot, with yogurt and a chopped salad. Musakhan is eaten with the hands: tear off bread soaked with onion and olive oil to wrap each bite of chicken.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: For musakhan rolls, shred the chicken, mix with the onions and roll in thin flatbread before baking until crisp.

recipes.name: Maqluba (upside-down rice with chicken, aubergine and cauliflower)
recipes.description: Layers of fried aubergine and cauliflower, chicken and spiced rice cooked in one pot in chicken stock, then flipped onto a platter to reveal a domed cake. A Friday family dish with a dramatic unveiling.
equipment: Large heavy non-stick pot (26 cm, at least 5 litres)
Deep pan or wok for frying

ingredients.name: Chicken legs or thighs, bone-in and skinless
Aubergines (2 medium)
ingredients.prep: cut into 1.5 cm rounds and salted

steps.t: Put the chicken in the large saucepan with the water, halved onion, cinnamon stick, cardamom, bay leaves, allspice and salt. Bring to the boil, skim off the foam, then simmer for 30 minutes, until the chicken is just cooked. Lift out the chicken, strain the stock and keep it hot; you need about 900 ml.

While the stock cooks, salt the aubergine slices for 20 minutes, then pat them dry. Heat the oil in the deep pan to 175 °C and fry the aubergine in batches for 3–4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden. Fry the cauliflower for 5–6 minutes, until golden brown at the edges. Drain everything on kitchen paper. (To roast instead, brush with oil and bake at 220 °C for 25 minutes.)

Line the base of the heavy pot with the tomato slices; they stop the rice sticking and look pretty when turned out. Arrange the chicken over them, then the aubergine and cauliflower in snug layers, tucking the garlic cloves in between.

Drain the rice, toss it with the turmeric, allspice, cinnamon and pepper and spread it evenly over the vegetables, pressing down gently. Pour in hot stock until it covers the rice by about 2 cm, then lay a small plate on top to hold the layers in place.

Bring to the boil, cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 30–35 minutes, until the rice is tender and the stock has been absorbed. Take off the heat and leave covered, untouched, for 15 minutes; this rest lets it hold its shape when turned out.
Meanwhile, melt the butter in a small pan and fry the almonds and pine nuts for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until golden.

Remove the lid and plate. Place the platter upside down over the pot and, holding both firmly with oven gloves, flip them over in one confident movement. Wait a minute, then lift the pot away slowly to reveal the maqluba ('upside down'). Scatter with the nuts and parsley and serve with yogurt and a chopped salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Msabbaha (warm chickpeas in tahini with garlic-lemon sauce)
recipes.description: Hummus's rustic cousin: soft, warm whole chickpeas folded through lemony tahini and topped with a sharp garlic, chilli and cumin sauce and olive oil. A favourite Jerusalem breakfast.

steps.t: Simmer the chickpeas in the water for 10–12 minutes, until very soft and hot all the way through. Drain, keeping about 150 ml of the cooking water.
While they cook, make the dakka: pound the garlic, chilli and salt in the mortar to a coarse paste, then stir in the lemon juice and cumin.
Mash about a quarter of the hot chickpeas in the bowl with the tahini, lemon juice, salt and a few tablespoons of the cooking water until it forms a loose, creamy sauce.
Fold in the remaining whole chickpeas with more cooking water as needed, so the msabbaha is spoonable and slightly soupy rather than stiff. Taste for salt and lemon.
Spoon into shallow bowls while warm. Top with the dakka, a generous pour of olive oil, parsley and a dusting of paprika.
Serve straight away with warm pita, raw onion wedges, pickles and fresh mint tea.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate covered for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently with a splash of water until hot throughout.

recipes.name: Mansaf (lamb in yogurt sauce with rice)
recipes.description: Jordan's national feast: lamb simmered until tender, then finished in a tangy yogurt sauce, served on thin bread and turmeric rice with toasted almonds and pine nuts, and plenty of extra sauce to pour over.

ingredients.name: Lamb shoulder or leg, in large pieces
ingredients.prep: boneless weight (bone-in pieces are traditional; use about 1.6 kg)

ingredients.name: Full-fat yogurt (or liquid jameed, see notes)

steps.t: Put the lamb in the stockpot, cover with the cold water and bring to the boil. Boil for 10 minutes, skimming off all the grey scum that rises, until the surface is clear.
Add the onion, cardamom, bay leaves, peppercorns, cinnamon stick and salt. Cover and simmer gently for 1½–2 hours, until the lamb is very tender. Lift out the meat and strain the broth.

For the sauce, whisk the yogurt and cornflour in the heavy pot until completely smooth; the cornflour stops it splitting. Set over medium heat and stir constantly in one direction with the wooden spoon for 10–15 minutes, until it comes to a gentle bubble. Then gradually stir in about 750 ml of the hot lamb broth until the sauce is the consistency of single cream.
Add the lamb to the sauce and simmer gently for 20–30 minutes, so the meat takes on the tangy flavour. Taste for salt.

Meanwhile, melt 3 tablespoons of ghee in the lidded saucepan, stir in the turmeric and the drained rice and stir for 2 minutes until coated. Add 900 ml of the lamb broth (topped up with water if needed) and the salt, bring to the boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 18–20 minutes. Rest, covered, for 10 minutes.
Toast the almonds and pine nuts in the remaining tablespoon of ghee over medium heat for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until golden.

Lay the bread over the serving tray and moisten it with a few ladles of sauce. Heap the rice on top, arrange the lamb over it and scatter with the nuts and parsley. Serve the rest of the sauce in bowls for everyone to pour over. Traditionally mansaf is eaten standing around the tray, with the right hand.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat the lamb in its sauce gently, stirring, until steaming hot (74 °C / 165 °F); reheat the rice separately.
notes: The authentic sauce uses jameed, dried salted fermented yogurt from Jordan's Karak region, soaked and blended with water; it is saltier and sharper, so season after adding it. Liquid jameed is sold in cartons in Middle Eastern shops.

recipes.name: Masgouf (Iraqi butterflied fish, oven-roasted)
recipes.description: Baghdad's riverside favourite: whole fish split open, rubbed with turmeric, tamarind and oil and roasted until smoky at the edges, then topped with tomato and onion. Adapted here for a hot home oven.

ingredients.name: Whole sea bass or carp (1.5 kg in total, 1 large or 2 small)

steps.t: Butterfly the fish, or ask your fishmonger to: cut along the back from head to tail, close to the backbone, and open it out flat like a book so it stays joined along the belly. Rinse and pat completely dry.
Mix the oil, tamarind, turmeric, curry powder, salt and pepper into a paste and rub it all over the flesh side. Leave for 20 minutes while the oven heats.
Heat the oven to 240 °C with a shelf near the top. Lay the fish skin side down on the lined tray, opened out flat.
Roast for 15 minutes, until the flesh has turned opaque and the edges are starting to colour.

Scatter the onion rings, tomato and pepper slices over the fish, drizzle with a little more oil and roast for 10–12 minutes more. Finish under a hot grill for 3–5 minutes for charred spots, until the flesh flakes easily at the thickest part (63 °C).
Bring the fish to the table on its tray with the flatbreads, lemon wedges and parsley. Everyone pulls the flesh off the bones with pieces of bread; serve with pickles and a chopped salad.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh; refrigerate leftovers off the bone for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently, covered, in a low oven until hot throughout.
notes: On the banks of the Tigris, carp is impaled on stakes and slow-cooked beside a wood fire; a charcoal grill with a hinged fish basket gives the closest result.

recipes.name: Iraqi kebab (lamb kebab with parsley and onion)
recipes.description: Juicy kebabs of minced lamb and beef with onion and parsley, grilled on flat skewers and wrapped in warm bread with grilled tomatoes, sumac onions and pickles, as in Baghdad's kebab shops.

steps.t: Grate the onion finely and squeeze it hard in the tea towel to remove as much juice as possible; discard the juice.

Put both meats in the bowl with the onion, parsley, garlic, baharat, salt and pepper. Knead for 4–5 minutes, until the mixture is sticky and holds together in one mass. Chill for 20–30 minutes if you have time; firm meat is easier to shape.
Light the charcoal and let it burn to glowing coals, or heat the oven grill to high. For the onion salad, toss the sliced onion with the sumac, parsley leaves and a pinch of salt.
Divide the meat into 8 portions. With wet hands, press each around a skewer into a kebab about 2 cm thick, squeezing it along the skewer so it holds tightly, and pinch the ends firmly onto the metal.
Grill for 8–10 minutes, turning every 2 minutes, until browned on all sides, juicy and cooked through to 71 °C. Grill the tomatoes alongside until soft and blackened in spots.

Warm the breads on the grill, then use one to pull the kebabs off each skewer. Serve wrapped in the bread with grilled tomatoes, sumac onions and pickles; amba (mango pickle sauce) is the classic Iraqi addition.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Chicken kabsa (Saudi spiced chicken and rice)
recipes.description: Saudi Arabia's everyday feast: chicken simmered with tomato, dried lime and warm whole spices, then long-grain rice cooked in the fragrant broth and heaped on a platter with fried almonds and raisins.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a tight lid

steps.t: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear, then leave it to soak in fresh water for 30 minutes while you cook the chicken.
Heat 4 tablespoons of oil in the large pot over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken pieces on all sides for about 8 minutes, in two batches if needed, then lift them out.

Add the onions to the pot and cook for 8 minutes, until golden. Add the garlic and chillies for 1 minute, then the whole spices for 30 seconds until fragrant, then the ground spices and tomato paste for 1 minute. Stir in the grated tomatoes and carrot and cook for 5 minutes, until thick and jammy.
Return the chicken, add the dried limes, water and salt and bring to the boil. Cover and simmer for 30 minutes, until the chicken is tender and cooked through to 74 °C.

Lift out the chicken. For crisp skin, brush it with oil and roast at 220 °C for 10–12 minutes while the rice cooks. Measure the broth: you need about 900 ml for 600 g of rice, so boil it down or top it up with water.

Bring the broth to the boil, add the drained rice and boil uncovered for 5 minutes, until the liquid has dropped to the level of the rice. Cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 20 minutes, until the rice is tender and every grain separate. Rest off the heat for 10 minutes.
Meanwhile, fry the almonds and raisins in 1 tablespoon of oil in the small frying pan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes, until the almonds are golden and the raisins puffed.

Heap the rice on the platter, removing the whole spices as you find them, set the chicken on top and scatter with the almonds and raisins. Serve with a tomato and cucumber salad, yogurt and a hot tomato and chilli sauce (daqoos).

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Lamb kabsa is made the same way: simmer lamb pieces for 1½ hours before adding the rice.

recipes.name: Chicken machboos (Gulf spiced rice with chicken and hashu)
recipes.description: The Gulf's signature rice: chicken cooked with deeply browned onions, bzar spices and dried limes, rice steamed in the broth with saffron and rose water, topped with sweet caramelised onions, chickpeas and raisins.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a tight lid

steps.t: Heat 3 tablespoons of ghee in the large pot over medium heat and fry the onions, stirring often, for 10–12 minutes, until a deep golden brown; this colour gives machboos its depth. Add the garlic, ginger and chillies for 1 minute, then the bzar, turmeric and whole spices for 30 seconds.

Add the chicken and turn it in the spiced onions for 5 minutes. Add the tomatoes, dried limes, water and salt, bring to the boil, then cover and simmer for 35–40 minutes, until the chicken is tender and cooked through to 74 °C.

Meanwhile, make the hashu: cook the sliced onion in 1 tablespoon of ghee in the frying pan over medium-low heat for 15 minutes, stirring, until soft and caramelised. Add the chickpeas, raisins, sugar, ground cardamom and 2 tablespoons of water and cook for 5 minutes, until glossy and sticky.
Lift the chicken out of the pot and keep it warm (or brown it under a hot grill for 5 minutes). Measure the broth, boiling it down or adding water to make about 900 ml, and bring it back to the boil.

Add the drained rice and boil uncovered for 5–6 minutes, until the liquid is level with the rice and small steam holes appear. Drizzle the saffron water, rose water and 1 tablespoon of ghee over the top, cover with a lid wrapped in the tea towel and cook on the lowest heat for 20–25 minutes, until the rice is tender and fluffy.

Spoon the rice onto a large platter, mixing the saffron streaks lightly, arrange the chicken on top and spoon over the hashu. Scatter with coriander and serve with salad, yogurt and daqoos (tomato and chilli sauce).

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Chicken mandi (Yemeni roast chicken on smoky rice)
recipes.description: Spice-rubbed chicken roasted above a tray of basmati so its juices drip into the rice, then smoked briefly with a glowing coal. A Hadhrami dish traditionally cooked in an underground oven, adapted for a home oven.
equipment: Wire rack that fits over the tin

steps.t: Mix the ground spices, garlic, salt and oil into a paste and rub it all over the chicken, under the skin as well. Leave for at least 1 hour, or overnight in the fridge.

Heat the oven to 200 °C. Set the roasting tin over medium heat on the hob, add 2 tablespoons of oil and cook the onion for 5 minutes until soft. Add the whole spices for 1 minute, then the drained rice, and stir for 2 minutes until coated.

Pour in the hot stock, add the dried limes and salt and bring to the boil. Set the rack over the tin and lay the chicken on it, skin side up, so its juices will drip onto the rice. Cover the whole tin tightly with foil.

Bake for 50 minutes. Uncover, brush the chicken with the melted ghee and turn the oven up to 220 °C. Roast for 20–25 minutes more, until the skin is deep golden, the thickest part of the thigh reaches 74 °C and the rice is tender, with crisp edges.

For the classic smoky flavour (optional), heat a piece of lump charcoal over a gas flame with tongs for 5–7 minutes until glowing. Set it in the small heatproof bowl in the middle of the rice, drop 1 teaspoon of ghee onto it and cover the tin tightly with foil for 10 minutes. Remove the coal carefully and do this only in a well-ventilated kitchen.
Fluff the rice, heap it onto a platter with the chicken on top and scatter with the almonds and raisins. Serve with zhug or a fresh tomato-chilli salsa and a green salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Saltah (Yemeni lamb stew with whipped fenugreek)
recipes.description: Yemen's national dish: a spicy, bubbling stew of lamb broth, potatoes, tomatoes and chilli brought to the table in a scorching pot and crowned with frothy whipped fenugreek (hulba).

ingredients.name: Ground fenugreek
ingredients.prep: soaked in 250 ml water for at least 4 hours

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander
ingredients.prep: pounded with the chilli and garlic

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 1.5 cm dice

steps.t: Start the hulba ahead: soak the ground fenugreek in 250 ml of water for at least 4 hours or overnight. The soaking draws out its bitterness; pour off the water before using.

For the broth, put the lamb in the stockpot with the water, halved onion, cardamom, peppercorns, turmeric and salt. Bring to the boil, skim, then simmer covered for about 1 hour, until the lamb is tender. Lift out the meat and shred it, and strain the broth.

Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the chopped onion for 6 minutes, until golden. Add the garlic, chillies, cumin and coriander for 1 minute, then the tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes, until soft.

Add the potatoes and about 500 ml of the broth and simmer for 15 minutes, until the potatoes are tender. Stir in the shredded lamb and mash a few potato pieces against the pan to thicken the stew. It should be thick but loose enough to bubble. Season with salt.

Whip the hulba: put the drained fenugreek in a bowl with 2–3 tablespoons of cold water and whisk hard for 5–8 minutes, adding cold water a spoonful at a time, until it turns pale, frothy and roughly doubles in volume. Pound the coriander, chilli, garlic and salt to a paste and whisk it in with the lemon juice.
Heat the cast-iron or stone pot over high heat until very hot. Tip in the stew so it boils fiercely, then spoon the hulba on top and carry it bubbling to the table.
Eat straight from the pot, scooping up the stew and froth with torn flatbread, with cups of the remaining hot broth to drink alongside.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the stew and broth within 2 hours and eat within 3 days; whip the hulba fresh.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Some cooks crack an egg or two into the bubbling stew just before adding the hulba.

recipes.name: Zhug (Yemeni green chilli and herb sauce)
recipes.description: A fiery green paste of fresh chillies, coriander, garlic, cumin and cardamom, called sahawiq in Yemen. Spooned onto stews, eggs, falafel, grilled meat and rice.
equipment: Food processor or large mortar and pestle

steps.t: For a milder zhug, scrape out some of the chilli seeds and white membranes before chopping. Wear gloves or wash your hands well afterwards.

Pulse the chillies, garlic, cumin, cardamom, black pepper and salt in the food processor until coarsely chopped, scraping down the sides. Traditionally it is pounded on a stone, which gives a slightly coarser paste.
Add the coriander and parsley and pulse until finely chopped but not completely smooth; you want some texture. Add the olive oil and lemon juice and pulse briefly to combine.
Taste and adjust the salt and lemon, then leave for 15 minutes for the flavours to blend. Serve with saltah, mandi, eggs, falafel or grilled meat, or stir a spoonful into yogurt as a dip.

recipes.storage: Keep in a jar under a thin layer of olive oil in the fridge for up to 1 week, or freeze in small portions.
notes: Red zhug is made the same way with red chillies.

recipes.name: Luqaimat (crisp dumplings with date syrup)
recipes.description: Small yeasted dumplings scented with cardamom and saffron, fried until crisp outside and airy within, then drizzled with date syrup and sesame. Made every evening in Ramadan across the Gulf.

steps.t: Whisk the flour, cornflour, yeast, sugar, salt and cardamom in the bowl. Add the saffron water, milk and water and beat with the whisk or a wooden spoon for 3–4 minutes into a smooth, thick, sticky batter, a little thicker than pancake batter.
Cover and leave in a warm place for about 1 hour, until doubled and full of bubbles. Stir it down briefly just before frying.
Pour the oil into the deep pan to about 6 cm deep, no more than one-third full, and heat to 170 °C on the thermometer.

Dip the two teaspoons in a cup of oil, scoop up a walnut-sized blob of batter with one and push it off into the oil with the other. (In Emirati homes the batter is squeezed out between thumb and forefinger.) Fry 10–12 at a time without crowding.

Fry for 5–7 minutes, turning them constantly with the slotted spoon so they colour evenly, until deep golden brown and crisp. They should sound hollow and feel light. Drain on a rack or kitchen paper and let the oil come back to 170 °C between batches.
While still hot, drizzle with the date syrup, toss to coat and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Serve immediately with Arabic coffee or karak chai; they are at their best within the hour.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within an hour; they soften as they stand.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a 200 °C oven for 5 minutes, then add the syrup.
notes: Sugar syrup flavoured with saffron and cardamom, or honey, can replace the date syrup.

recipes.name: Karak chai (strong cardamom tea with evaporated milk)
recipes.description: Black tea boiled hard with cardamom until strong ('karak'), then simmered with evaporated milk and sugar into a rich caramel-coloured brew. Sold from roadside cafeterias all over the Gulf.

ingredients.name: Strong loose black tea (or 4 tea bags)

steps.t: Bring the water to the boil in the saucepan with the crushed cardamom (and saffron, if using) and boil for 3 minutes, so the cardamom flavours the water.
Add the tea and boil hard for 3–4 minutes, until the liquid is very dark, almost black; this long boil is what makes it karak, or strong.

Stir in the evaporated milk and sugar and bring back to the boil over medium heat. Watch closely: as it rises, lift the pan off the heat or lower it, let the foam settle, then bring it up again. Repeat 2–3 times over 3–4 minutes, until the tea is a deep caramel colour and slightly thickened.
Pour through the strainer into small glasses or cups and serve very hot, with luqaimat, biscuits or a chapati sandwich.

recipes.storage: Best made fresh.

recipes.name: Balaleet (sweet saffron vermicelli with omelette)
recipes.description: Toasted vermicelli sweetened with sugar, cardamom, saffron and rose water, topped with a thin savoury omelette. A sweet-and-salty Emirati breakfast, also served on Eid mornings.
equipment: Non-stick frying pan with a lid

steps.t: Stir the rose water into the steeped saffron and set aside.

Melt 2 tablespoons of ghee in the saucepan over medium heat. Add the broken vermicelli and stir constantly for 3–4 minutes, until evenly golden brown and smelling nutty; it can burn quickly at the end.
Carefully pour in the boiling water (it will spit), stir and cook for 3–4 minutes, until the vermicelli is just tender. If much water remains, pour it off.

Stir in the sugar, cardamom and saffron-rose water and cook over low heat for 2–3 minutes, stirring gently, until the sugar has dissolved and the vermicelli is glossy and golden. Cover and keep warm off the heat.

Whisk the eggs with the salt (and a few saffron threads for colour if you like). Melt the remaining ghee in the frying pan over medium-low heat, pour in the eggs and cook, covered, for 3–4 minutes, until set right through. Slide out and cut into wedges or strips.
Spoon the warm vermicelli into bowls, lay the omelette on top and scatter with pistachios. Serve with sweet tea or karak chai.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh; the vermicelli keeps 2 days refrigerated.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the vermicelli with a splash of water until hot; make the omelette fresh.

recipes.name: Plov (Uzbek lamb, carrot and rice pilaf)
recipes.description: Uzbekistan's national dish, called osh at home: lamb and a mountain of carrot matchsticks slowly cooked with cumin into a rich base (zirvak), then rice steamed on top with whole heads of garlic buried inside.
equipment: Heavy cast-iron pot or kazan (6 litres) with a lid

ingredients.name: Carrots (yellow and orange)
ingredients.prep: cut into 5 mm matchsticks, not grated

ingredients.name: Medium-grain rice (devzira or Calrose)
ingredients.prep: rinsed and soaked in warm salted water for 1 hour

ingredients.name: Whole heads of garlic (2)
ingredients.prep: loose papery skin rubbed off, left whole

steps.t: Rinse the rice in several changes of water until it runs clear and soak it in warm salted water for 1 hour. Cut the carrots into long matchsticks by hand; grated carrot turns to mush.

Heat the oil in the kazan over high heat until it shimmers and just starts to smoke. Fry the lamb in two batches, turning, for 8–10 minutes, until a deep brown crust forms on all sides. Return all the meat to the pot.

Add the onions and fry for 8–10 minutes, stirring, until golden brown. Spread the carrots over the top in a thick layer and leave them for 2–3 minutes without stirring, then stir and fry for 10 minutes more, until softened, glossy and turning golden.

Rub the cumin seeds between your palms over the pot to release their aroma, then add the coriander, whole chillies, barberries, drained chickpeas and 2 teaspoons of the salt. Pour in enough boiling water to just cover, bring to the boil and simmer gently, partly covered, for 45–60 minutes, until the lamb is tender. This rich base is the zirvak.

Turn the heat up. Drain the rice and spread it evenly over the zirvak without stirring. Pour boiling water gently over the back of the slotted spoon so the rice is not disturbed, until it is covered by about 1.5 cm. Add the remaining salt and press the whole garlic heads into the centre of the rice.

Boil hard, uncovered, for 10–12 minutes, until the water has sunk below the surface of the rice. Gather the rice into a dome with the slotted spoon and poke 6–8 holes down to the bottom with the handle of a wooden spoon so steam can rise.
Cover tightly (a plate under the lid helps) and cook on the lowest heat for 25–30 minutes, until the rice is tender and fluffy. Turn off the heat and rest for 10 minutes without lifting the lid.

Fold the rice and carrots together gently from the sides, then heap them on the platter. Arrange the lamb and the soft garlic heads on top. Serve with achichuk (sliced tomato, onion and chilli salad), non bread and green tea.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Some regions add raisins or quince; in Samarkand the layers are not mixed before serving.

recipes.name: Samsa (Uzbek flaky lamb and onion pastries)
recipes.description: Triangular pastries of buttery, spiral-layered dough filled with diced lamb, plenty of onion, cumin and black pepper, baked until shatteringly flaky. Sold hot from tandoor ovens across Central Asia.
equipment: Baking trays lined with baking paper

ingredients.name: Lamb shoulder with some of its fat
ingredients.prep: cut into 5 mm dice (or coarse lamb mince)

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt with the cold water and knead for 8–10 minutes into a firm, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 30 minutes so it relaxes and rolls out thinly.

Roll the dough out on a lightly floured surface as thinly as you can, into a rectangle about 50 × 60 cm. Spread the soft butter over the whole surface, then roll it up tightly from a long side into a log. Cut it into 12 pieces, wrap and chill for 30 minutes to firm the butter; this creates the flaky spiral layers.
For the filling, mix the diced lamb with the onions, crushed cumin, pepper, salt and cold water. The filling goes in raw; the onion juices keep it moist as it bakes.
Heat the oven to 200 °C. Stand each piece of dough on a cut side and press it flat with your palm so the spiral faces up, then roll it into a 12–13 cm round, thinner at the edges than in the centre.

Put 2 heaped tablespoons of filling in the centre. Fold three sides up over the filling to meet in the middle, forming a triangle, and pinch the seams tightly closed. Set seam side down on the lined trays.
Brush with the beaten egg, sprinkle with sesame or nigella seeds and bake for 25–30 minutes, until deep golden and flaky and the filling is sizzling; the centre of the filling should reach 71 °C.
Cool for 5 minutes, as the juices inside are very hot, and serve warm with green tea and a tomato and onion salad.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days; unbaked samsa freeze well (bake from frozen, adding 10 minutes).
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a 180 °C oven for 10–12 minutes until hot throughout; a microwave makes the pastry soft.
notes: Pumpkin samsa (with diced squash, onion and a little butter) is the autumn vegetarian version.

recipes.name: Laghman (Uyghur hand-pulled noodles with lamb and vegetables)
recipes.description: Springy hand-pulled noodles topped with a stir-fried sauce of lamb, peppers, celery, green beans and tomato, seasoned with cumin, garlic and black vinegar. The great noodle dish of the Uyghurs.

steps.t: Dissolve the salt and bicarbonate of soda in the water and mix it into the flour to a shaggy dough. Knead for 10 minutes, rest it covered for 20 minutes, then knead again for 5 minutes, until very smooth and elastic. Cover and rest for 30 minutes more; the long rests relax the gluten so the noodles stretch without snapping.

Divide the dough into 12–16 pieces and roll each into a rope as thick as a pencil and about 15 cm long. Coat them well with oil, coil them on the oiled plate, cover with cling film and rest for at least 30 minutes, or up to 2 hours.

For the topping, heat the oil in the wok over high heat and stir-fry the lamb for 2–3 minutes, until browned. Add the onion and garlic for 2 minutes, then the cumin and tomato paste for 1 minute. Add the peppers, celery, beans and chilli and stir-fry for 3 minutes.
Add the tomatoes, soy sauce, salt and water and simmer for 8–10 minutes, until the vegetables are tender-crisp and the sauce has thickened and turned glossy. Stir in the vinegar and keep warm.

Bring a large pot of water to the boil. Pick up a rope by both ends and stretch it gently, bouncing the middle on the work surface, until it is 1–1.5 metres long and 3–4 mm thick; loop it around your hands and keep stretching if it is still thick. Drop it straight into the boiling water and repeat with the rest, working in batches.
Boil for 2–3 minutes, until the noodles float and are tender but chewy. Lift them into a bowl of cold water for a few seconds to firm them, then drain and toss with a few drops of oil.
Divide the noodles between bowls and ladle the hot lamb and vegetable sauce over them. Serve with more vinegar, crushed garlic and chilli oil at the table.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the sauce and noodles separately within 2 hours and eat within 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the sauce until steaming hot throughout; dip the noodles in boiling water for 30 seconds.
notes: Short of time, use 500 g of fresh thick wheat noodles or dried lamian noodles instead of pulling your own.

recipes.name: Shurpa (Uzbek lamb and vegetable soup)
recipes.description: A clear, golden lamb broth with large pieces of meat, potatoes, carrots, peppers, tomatoes and chickpeas, finished with dill and coriander. Simple, restorative Central Asian home cooking.

ingredients.name: Lamb shoulder or neck
ingredients.prep: in large pieces (bone-in pieces are traditional)

steps.t: Put the lamb in the stockpot with the cold water and bring slowly to the boil over medium heat. As it comes up, skim off all the grey foam for about 10 minutes, until the surface is clean; this keeps the broth clear.

Add the drained chickpeas, the whole onion, the bay leaves and peppercorns. Lower the heat so the broth barely trembles and simmer, partly covered, for 1–1½ hours, until the lamb is tender. Hard boiling makes the broth cloudy.
Remove and discard the whole onion. Add the carrots, pepper, tomatoes and sliced onion and simmer for 15 minutes.
Add the potatoes, cumin, ground coriander and salt and simmer for 20 minutes more, until the potatoes are tender but still whole.
Lift out the lamb, cut it into portions and return it to the pot with the garlic and whole chilli. Simmer for 5 minutes and taste for salt.
Ladle into deep bowls so everyone gets a piece of meat, potato and vegetables. Scatter generously with dill and coriander and serve with non bread and thinly sliced raw onion.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days, or freeze the broth for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Sabich (pita with fried aubergine, egg and tahini)
recipes.description: Pita stuffed with fried aubergine, sliced hard-boiled egg, tahini, chopped salad and tangy amba. Brought to Israel by Iraqi Jews as a Shabbat breakfast and now a beloved street sandwich.

steps.t: Sprinkle the aubergine slices with the salt and leave them in a colander for 20 minutes to draw out moisture, then pat them completely dry with kitchen paper.
Lower the eggs into a saucepan of boiling water and cook for 9–10 minutes for firm yolks. Cool them in iced water, peel and slice.

Heat about 1 cm of oil in the frying pan to 175 °C, or until a piece of aubergine sizzles at once. Fry the slices in batches for 3–4 minutes per side, until deep golden outside and creamy all the way through. Drain on kitchen paper.
Whisk the tahini with the lemon juice and garlic, then whisk in the cold water a spoonful at a time until smooth and pourable; it thickens before it loosens. Season with salt.
Mix the tomatoes, cucumber, onion and parsley with the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.

Warm the pitas and open the pockets. Spread tahini inside, add a few slices of aubergine and egg and a spoonful of salad, then repeat the layers. Finish with more tahini, amba and zhug and eat straight away, with extra napkins.

recipes.storage: Assemble just before eating; fried aubergine and boiled eggs keep 2 days refrigerated.
notes: Amba, a pickled mango sauce with fenugreek and turmeric, is sold in jars in Middle Eastern shops.

recipes.name: Israeli salad (finely chopped cucumber and tomato salad)
recipes.description: Cucumbers and tomatoes diced very small and evenly, with onion and parsley, dressed simply with lemon and olive oil. Eaten at almost every Israeli meal, from breakfast to falafel.

steps.t: Cut the cucumbers and tomatoes into small, even dice about 5 mm across. The fine, uniform cut is what makes this salad; take your time and use a sharp knife so the tomatoes don't bleed.
Dice the onion as finely as you can and chop the parsley. Put everything in the bowl.
Just before serving, add the lemon juice, olive oil, salt and pepper and toss gently. Salt draws out the vegetables' juices, so don't dress it ahead.
Serve straight away, at breakfast with eggs, labneh and bread, or alongside falafel, schnitzel or sabich. A pinch of sumac or za'atar on top is a popular addition.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately; undressed, the chopped vegetables keep a few hours in the fridge.

recipes.name: Jachnun (slow-baked rolled Yemenite pastry)
recipes.description: Paper-thin layers of buttery dough rolled into logs and baked overnight at a low heat until deep amber, flaky and slightly sweet. The Yemenite-Jewish Shabbat breakfast, served with grated tomato, zhug and slow-baked eggs.
equipment: Heavy ovenproof pot with a tight lid (about 24 cm)

ingredients.name: Margarine (traditional, keeps it pareve) or butter

steps.t: Mix the flour, sugar and salt in a bowl, add the water and knead for 10 minutes into a very smooth, soft, elastic dough that is slightly sticky. Divide it into 6 balls, coat each with a little margarine, cover and rest for 1 hour (or overnight in the fridge).

Grease a large work surface and your hands with margarine. Flatten a ball and stretch it outwards with your fingertips and the backs of your hands into a very thin rectangle about 50 × 40 cm, so thin that you can see the surface through it. Small tears don't matter.

Spread the sheet thinly with soft margarine. Fold the long sides in towards the middle in thirds to make a strip about 10 cm wide, spread it with a little more margarine, then roll it up tightly from a short end into a log. Repeat with the other balls.

Line the pot with baking paper and pack the logs in snugly side by side. Nestle the washed eggs in their shells between and on top of the rolls. Cover with another sheet of baking paper, then foil, then the lid, sealing tightly so no steam escapes.

Bake at 100 °C for 10 hours, overnight, or between 8 and 12 hours. The jachnun is ready when it is a deep caramel brown, crisp on the outside and flaky within; the eggs inside turn creamy with beige whites.
Serve hot from the pot with the peeled brown eggs, freshly grated tomato seasoned with a pinch of salt, and zhug for spooning over each bite.

recipes.storage: Cool, wrap and refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze the shaped, unbaked logs for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Warm, covered, in a 150 °C oven for 15 minutes.
notes: Kubaneh (a domed yeasted bread) and malawach (pan-fried layered flatbread) are made from similar buttery Yemenite doughs.

recipes.name: Kabuli pulao (Afghan lamb rice with carrots and raisins)
recipes.description: Afghanistan's national dish: tender lamb hidden under rice cooked in a dark, onion-rich broth with warm spices, crowned with sweet caramelised carrot strips, raisins, almonds and pistachios.
equipment: Large heavy ovenproof pot with a lid

ingredients.name: Lamb shoulder or shank
ingredients.prep: boneless weight, in large pieces (bone-in is traditional)

ingredients.name: Aged long-grain basmati or sella rice

steps.t: Heat 6 tablespoons of oil in the heavy pot over medium heat and fry the onions, stirring often, for 12–15 minutes, until a deep, even brown; this is what gives the rice its rich colour. Don't let them blacken.

Add the lamb and brown it with the onions for 8–10 minutes. Stir in the cumin, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, pepper and salt, pour in the water and bring to the boil. Cover and simmer for 1–1½ hours, until the lamb is tender.

Meanwhile, heat 2 tablespoons of oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the carrots for 5–7 minutes, until tender and lightly caramelised. Sprinkle with the sugar, cook for 1 minute more and lift them out. In the same pan, fry the raisins for 1–2 minutes until they puff, then the almonds and pistachios for 2 minutes until lightly toasted.

Heat the oven to 150 °C. Lift the lamb out of the pot and measure the broth: you need about 1.2 litres for 800 g of rice, so top up with water or boil it down. Bring it back to the boil, add the drained rice and boil uncovered for 6–8 minutes, until the liquid has been absorbed and small steam holes appear on the surface.

Push the lamb down into the rice, or lay it on top, and pile the carrots and raisins over the rice. Cover with a lid wrapped in the tea towel and bake for 40 minutes (or cook on the lowest heat on the hob), until the rice is tender and every grain separate.

To serve, spoon the topping aside, heap the rice on the platter with the lamb buried in the centre, and cover with the carrots, raisins and nuts. Serve with a tomato and onion salad, yogurt and green chutney.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Mantu (Afghan beef dumplings with yogurt and split pea sauce)
recipes.description: Steamed dumplings filled with spiced beef and onion, served on garlicky strained yogurt and topped with a tomato and yellow split pea sauce, dried mint and chilli. A centrepiece of Afghan celebrations.

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt, then add the egg and water and knead for 8–10 minutes into a firm, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

For the filling, heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions for 5 minutes until soft. Add the beef and garlic and cook for 8–10 minutes, breaking it up, until no pink remains and the liquid has evaporated. Season with the coriander, pepper and salt and leave to cool.

For the sauce, simmer the split peas in plenty of water for 25–30 minutes, until tender but holding their shape, then drain. Heat the oil in the saucepan, fry the garlic for 30 seconds, add the tomato paste and grated tomato and cook for 3 minutes. Add the split peas, chilli, salt and 200 ml of water and simmer for 10 minutes into a thick sauce.

Roll the dough out on a floured surface as thinly as you can, about 1 mm, and cut it into 8 cm squares. Put a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre of each. Bring two opposite corners up over the filling and pinch them together, then bring up the other two corners and pinch all the edges together to make a little four-cornered parcel.

Oil the steamer tiers and arrange the mantu 1 cm apart. Steam over rapidly boiling water for 25–30 minutes, until the dough is translucent and tender. (With shop-bought wonton wrappers, 12–15 minutes is enough.)
Mix the yogurt with the crushed garlic, a pinch of salt and a little water so it spreads easily.

Spread half the yogurt over a warm platter, arrange the mantu on top and spoon over the rest of the yogurt and the hot split pea sauce. Sprinkle with dried mint, chilli flakes and coriander and serve straight away.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days; keep the sauces separately. Uncooked mantu freeze well on a tray.
recipes.reheating: Re-steam for 5–8 minutes until hot throughout and reheat the sauce until steaming.
notes: Many Afghan cooks use square wonton wrappers instead of homemade dough; the filling is the same.

recipes.name: Bolani (Afghan flatbread stuffed with potato and leek)
recipes.description: Thin half-moon flatbreads filled with potato mashed with leek, coriander and chilli, fried until blistered and crisp. Sold on Kabul's streets and made at home for Eid and picnics, with yogurt and chutney.
equipment: Large heavy frying pan or griddle

ingredients.name: Gandana (Afghan leek), or the white and pale green of leeks
Plain yogurt
ingredients.prep: mixed with a pinch of salt and dried mint

steps.t: Mix the flour, salt, oil and water and knead for 8 minutes into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Boil the potatoes in salted water for 15–20 minutes, until completely tender, then drain well and mash. Wash the sliced leeks thoroughly to remove grit, squeeze them dry and stir them into the hot mash with the coriander, chilli, ground coriander, salt and pepper. Leave to cool.
Divide the dough into 8 balls. Roll each out on a floured surface into a thin round about 22 cm across and 1–2 mm thick.

Spread about 4 tablespoons of filling over one half of a round, leaving a 1 cm border. Fold the other half over to make a half-moon, press out any air and seal the edge firmly with your fingers or a fork. Prick the top a few times. Keep shaped bolani under a cloth while you make the rest.

Heat the frying pan over medium-high heat with about 1 tablespoon of oil. Fry the bolani one or two at a time for 2–3 minutes per side, brushing the top with oil before turning, until golden, blistered and crisp, and the dough is cooked through.
Cut into wedges and serve hot with the minty yogurt and a green chilli and coriander chutney.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate cooled bolani for up to 3 days, or freeze for a month.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a dry frying pan or 200 °C oven for 4–5 minutes until hot through.
notes: A pumpkin filling (kadu) or a lentil filling are other favourites.

recipes.name: Khachapuri adjaruli (Georgian cheese boats with egg)
recipes.description: Boat-shaped yeasted breads filled with molten salty cheese, finished with a runny egg yolk and a pat of butter to stir in at the table. The famous bread of Georgia's Black Sea coast.
equipment: Baking trays lined with baking paper

ingredients.name: Eggs
ingredients.prep: separated: whites into the cheese, yolks kept whole

steps.t: Stir the yeast and sugar into the warm milk and water and leave for 5 minutes until foamy. Add the flour, salt and oil and knead for 8–10 minutes into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and leave in a warm place for about 1 hour, until doubled.

Mix the grated sulguni or mozzarella and the crumbled cheese with the egg whites to a thick, moist paste. If your feta is very salty, soak it in cold water for 15 minutes first and squeeze it dry. Keep each yolk in its half shell or a small cup.
Put two baking trays in the oven and heat it to 240 °C. Divide the dough into 6 pieces and roll each into an oval about 25 × 15 cm on a floured sheet of baking paper.
Roll the two long sides in towards the centre to form thick raised rims, leaving a wide gap in the middle, then pinch the two ends together and twist them into points so the bread looks like a boat.

Fill each boat with the cheese mixture, keeping it off the rims, and brush the rims with a little milk. Slide the breads on their paper onto the hot trays and bake for 10–12 minutes, until the crust is golden and the cheese is bubbling.
Take them out, make a well in the cheese of each with a spoon and slip in an egg yolk. Return to the oven for 1–2 minutes, just to warm the yolk; it should stay runny.
Put a pat of butter on each and serve at once. At the table, stir the yolk and butter into the hot cheese and tear off pieces of crust to dip.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately; leftovers keep 2 days refrigerated.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a 180 °C oven for 6–8 minutes until hot throughout.
notes: For imeruli khachapuri, enclose the same cheese filling in a round of dough and bake or pan-fry it flat.

recipes.name: Khinkali (Georgian soup dumplings with beef and lamb)
recipes.description: Large pleated dumplings filled with peppery minced beef and lamb, onion and herbs, which turn into a pocket of hot broth as they boil. Eaten by hand: hold the knot, bite, sip the juices, then eat.

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt with the water and knead for 10 minutes into a stiff, smooth dough; khinkali dough is firmer than most so it can hold the juices. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

For the filling, mix the meats, onion, garlic, coriander, caraway, chilli, pepper and salt in the bowl. Add the cold water a little at a time, squeezing and working the mixture with your hand for 3–4 minutes, until all the water is absorbed and the filling is loose and sloppy. This water becomes the broth inside.
Roll the dough out on a floured surface to about 2 mm thick and cut out 10 cm rounds (re-roll the scraps once). Roll the edges of each round a little thinner than the centre. You should get about 20.

Put a heaped tablespoon of filling in the centre of a round. Holding it in one hand, lift the edge with the other and fold it into small pleats, rotating as you go, making 15–20 pleats that gather above the filling. Pinch and twist the pleats together at the top to seal them into a knot, and set the dumpling on a floured tray. Repeat.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to the boil and stir it gently. Lower in about 10 khinkali, stir once so they don't stick, and boil for 10–12 minutes from when they float, until the dough is tender and the filling is cooked through (71 °C).

Lift them out with the slotted spoon onto a platter, grind over plenty of black pepper and serve at once. To eat, pick one up by its knot, bite a small hole, sip the broth, then eat the rest, leaving the doughy knot on the plate.

recipes.storage: Freeze uncooked khinkali on a floured tray, then bag them; boil from frozen for 15 minutes. Cooked leftovers keep 2 days refrigerated.
recipes.reheating: Pan-fry cooked khinkali in a little butter until golden and hot through.

recipes.name: Chakhokhbili (Georgian chicken and tomato stew with herbs)
recipes.description: Chicken braised with lots of onions and ripe tomatoes, garlic, blue fenugreek and coriander, finished with a big handful of fresh herbs. A homely Georgian stew to mop up with bread.
equipment: Heavy pot or deep frying pan with a lid

ingredients.name: Chicken thighs and drumsticks, bone-in and skinless
Blue fenugreek (utskho suneli), or ground fenugreek

steps.t: Peel the tomatoes: cut a small cross in the base of each, cover with boiling water for 30–60 seconds until the skin starts to curl, then drain and slip off the skins. Chop the flesh, keeping the juice.

Heat the heavy pot over medium-high heat and add the chicken in a single layer with no fat; let it sear and release its juices for 8–10 minutes, turning once, until golden in places. Add the butter and onions and cook for 10 minutes, stirring, until the onions are soft and golden.
Add the tomatoes and their juice, half the garlic, the chilli, ground coriander, fenugreek, paprika, bay leaf, salt and pepper. Stir well and bring to a simmer.

Cover and cook on low heat for 25–30 minutes, stirring now and then, until the chicken is tender, reaches 74 °C near the bone and the sauce has thickened. Uncover for the last few minutes if it is watery.
Stir in the chopped herbs and the remaining garlic and simmer for 2 minutes, then take off the heat and rest for 10 minutes so the herbs perfume the sauce.
Serve hot in deep plates with plenty of Georgian bread (shoti or tonis puri) or crusty bread, or with mchadi cornbread and a cucumber and tomato salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: The name comes from khokhobi, pheasant, the original bird; a whole chicken cut into pieces with its skin gives a richer sauce.

recipes.name: Lobio (Georgian spiced kidney beans with walnuts and coriander)
recipes.description: Red kidney beans cooked until creamy, then roughly mashed with fried onions, a garlic and walnut paste, blue fenugreek and lots of coriander. Served hot in clay pots with cornbread and pickles.

ingredients.name: Blue fenugreek (utskho suneli), or ground fenugreek

steps.t: Drain the soaked beans, put them in the saucepan with the bay leaf and cover with fresh water by 5 cm. Bring to the boil and boil hard for 10 minutes, skimming off the foam; red kidney beans must boil vigorously to destroy their natural toxins.

Lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, for 1–1½ hours, until the beans are very soft and creamy inside. Top up with boiling water as needed so they stay covered. Drain, keeping the cooking liquid.
Meanwhile, heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and fry the onions for 10–12 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden.
Pound the walnuts, garlic, salt, ground coriander, fenugreek, savory and chilli in the mortar to a coarse, oily paste.

Return the beans to the pan and mash about half of them roughly with the potato masher, leaving the rest whole. Stir in the fried onions, the walnut paste and enough cooking liquid to make a thick, rustic stew. Simmer gently for 5–10 minutes, stirring, so the flavours combine.
Off the heat, stir in the coriander, parsley and vinegar. Taste for salt and sharpness.
Serve hot or warm, in clay bowls if you have them, with mchadi (cornbread) or bread, pickled vegetables and a plate of fresh herbs and radishes.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Loosen with water and reheat until steaming hot throughout (74 °C / 165 °F); add fresh coriander before serving.
notes: With canned beans (3 cans, drained), skip the first two steps and mash them with a little water.

recipes.name: Kharcho (Georgian beef soup with walnuts, rice and sour plum)
recipes.description: A thick, warming beef soup with rice, soured with tkemali plum sauce and enriched with a paste of walnuts, garlic and Georgian spices, finished with a heap of coriander. Tangy, nutty and gently hot.
equipment: Mortar and pestle or food processor

ingredients.name: Blue fenugreek (utskho suneli), or ground fenugreek
Tkemali (sour plum sauce), or tamarind paste

steps.t: Put the beef in the stockpot with the cold water and bring to the boil, skimming off the foam for 5–10 minutes until the surface is clear. Add the bay leaves and peppercorns, cover and simmer gently for 1½ hours, until the beef is tender.
Meanwhile, heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions for 10 minutes, until soft and golden. Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes until it darkens.
Add the onions and the rinsed rice to the broth and simmer for 15 minutes.
Pound the walnuts with 4 of the garlic cloves, the coriander, fenugreek, paprika, chilli and salt to a coarse paste (or pulse in a food processor). Loosen it with a ladle of hot broth.

Stir the walnut paste and the tkemali into the soup and simmer for 5–10 minutes, until the rice is tender and the soup has thickened slightly. Taste: it should be sour, nutty and gently spicy, so add more tkemali or salt as needed.
Take off the heat, stir in the remaining garlic (crushed) and the herbs, and rest for 5 minutes. Serve hot with Georgian bread or crusty bread.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Loosen with water and reheat until steaming hot throughout (74 °C / 165 °F).
notes: Tkemali is a Georgian sauce of sour cherry plums, sold in bottles; tamarind paste or a little pomegranate molasses with lemon gives a similar sourness.

recipes.name: Ghapama (pumpkin stuffed with rice, dried fruit and honey)
recipes.description: A whole pumpkin filled with buttery rice, dried apricots, prunes, raisins, walnuts, honey and cinnamon, baked until the flesh is soft enough to cut in wedges. An Armenian New Year and Christmas centrepiece.

ingredients.name: Whole round pumpkin (about 3 kg)
ingredients.prep: lid cut off, seeds and fibres scraped out

steps.t: Heat the oven to 180 °C. Wash the pumpkin and cut a lid around the stalk, about 12 cm across, angling the knife inwards so the lid sits back securely. Scrape out all the seeds and stringy fibres with a large spoon. Rub the inside with 1 tablespoon of the honey and the salt.
Bring a saucepan of salted water to the boil, add the rice and boil for 6–8 minutes, until half-cooked: soft outside but still firm in the middle. Drain well.
Mix the rice with the dried apricots, prunes, raisins, walnuts and cinnamon, then stir in most of the melted butter and 2 tablespoons of honey.
Spoon the filling into the pumpkin, filling it loosely to about 3 cm below the rim, as the rice swells. Drizzle over the water, the remaining butter and honey, and put the lid back on.

Set the pumpkin on the baking tray and bake for 1½–2 hours, depending on its size, until a skewer slides easily through the side of the pumpkin and the rice inside is tender. If the skin darkens too much, cover it loosely with foil.

Rest for 10 minutes, then carry it to the table whole. Cut it from top to bottom into wedges, so that everyone gets both soft pumpkin and fruity rice, and drizzle with a little more honey if you like.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat wedges, covered, in a 180 °C oven for 15–20 minutes until hot throughout.
notes: A dense, sweet pumpkin such as Crown Prince or kabocha works best; carving pumpkins are watery.

recipes.name: Shah plov (Azerbaijani crown pilaf in a lavash crust)
recipes.description: Saffron rice layered with lamb braised with dried apricots, raisins and prunes, sealed inside buttery lavash and baked into a golden dome, then turned out and cut like a crown. Azerbaijan's festive royal pilaf.
equipment: Deep heavy ovenproof pot or round tin (24 cm)

ingredients.name: Saffron threads
ingredients.prep: ground and steeped in 4 tbsp hot water

steps.t: Melt 2 tablespoons of butter in the frying pan over medium-high heat and brown the lamb in batches for 8–10 minutes. Add the onions and cook for 10 minutes, until soft and golden. Stir in the turmeric, cinnamon, salt and pepper, add the water, cover and simmer for 1 hour, until the lamb is tender and the liquid has reduced to a little thick sauce. Stir in the dried fruit for the last 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, bring 3 litres of water with the 2 tablespoons of salt to the boil. Add the drained rice and boil for 6–7 minutes, until just al dente, then drain. Toss it gently with the saffron water and 3 tablespoons of the melted butter.

Heat the oven to 180 °C. Brush the pot generously with butter. Cut the lavash into wide strips and line the pot with them, radiating from the centre of the base and overlapping, leaving about 10 cm hanging over the rim. Brush each layer with butter and make two layers in all.

Spread a third of the rice over the base and press it down lightly. Add half the lamb and fruit, then another third of the rice, the rest of the filling and the last of the rice. Fold the overhanging lavash over the top, patching any gaps with extra pieces, brush with butter and pour the remaining butter over.
Cover with a lid or foil and bake for 45 minutes, then uncover and bake for 15–20 minutes more, until the crust is deep golden and crisp; lift the edge with a knife to check the sides.

Rest for 10 minutes, then set a large platter over the pot and turn the plov out in one confident movement. Cut a circle in the top crust and lift it like a crown, or cut the whole dome into wedges at the table. Serve with a herb salad and pickles.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Roasted chestnuts are a classic addition to the filling. Some cooks make the crust from a simple dough (qazmaq) rolled thin instead of lavash.

recipes.name: Göyərti qutabı (Azerbaijani thin flatbreads filled with herbs)
recipes.description: Paper-thin half-moons of unleavened dough filled with spinach, coriander, dill and spring onion, cooked on a dry griddle and brushed with butter. Served warm with yogurt and sumac.
equipment: Large heavy frying pan, griddle or saj

steps.t: Mix the flour, salt, oil and warm water and knead for 8 minutes into a firm, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 30 minutes so it rolls out paper-thin.

Mix the chopped spinach and herbs with the salt and squeeze them gently with your hands for a minute so they wilt and release their liquid; pour off the liquid. Stir in the spring onions, sumac and pepper.
Divide the dough into 12 balls. Roll each on a lightly floured surface into a very thin round, about 1 mm thick and 18–20 cm across.

Spread a thin layer of filling over one half of a round, fold the other half over and press the edges together, pushing out any air. Trim the edge with a small plate and a knife for a neat half-moon, or crimp it with your fingers.
Heat the dry frying pan or griddle over medium-high heat. Cook the qutab one or two at a time for 1–2 minutes per side, until the dough is cooked, dry and speckled with brown spots; don't add oil.
Brush each one with melted butter as it comes off the pan and stack them so they stay soft. Sprinkle with sumac and serve warm with yogurt for dipping.

recipes.storage: Best eaten warm; leftovers keep 2 days refrigerated.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a dry frying pan for 1 minute per side.
notes: Meat qutab are filled with lamb mince, onion and pomegranate seeds; pumpkin qutab with squash cooked with onion and cinnamon.

recipes.name: Sindhi biryani
recipes.description: Sindh's bold, tangy biryani: sour-yogurt chicken layered with basmati, fried potatoes, sliced tomatoes, dried plums, mint and plenty of green chillies, then steamed on dum.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a tight lid

ingredients.name: Sindhi biryani masala or garam masala
Aloo bukhara (dried plums)
ingredients.prep: soaked in warm water for 10 minutes

ingredients.name: Saffron (or a few drops of yellow food colour)

steps.t: Rinse the basmati in several changes of cold water until the water runs almost clear, then leave it to soak in fresh water for 30 minutes. Soak the aloo bukhara in a small bowl of warm water, and crumble the saffron into the warm milk to steep.

Mix the chicken with the yogurt, ginger and garlic pastes, chilli powder, ground coriander, turmeric, half the biryani masala and the salt. Leave to marinate for at least 30 minutes, or covered in the fridge for up to 12 hours; the slightly sour yogurt gives Sindhi biryani its tang.

Heat the oil in the large heavy pot over medium-high heat. Fry the potato halves, turning them, until golden on all sides but still firm in the centre, 6–8 minutes, then lift them out with a slotted spoon. They finish cooking in the steam later.

Add the onions to the same oil and fry, stirring more often as they colour, until evenly deep golden brown, 12–15 minutes. Lift out about a third onto kitchen paper for layering. Add the cinnamon, bay leaves, cloves, both cardamoms, peppercorns and cumin seeds to the pot and stir for 30 seconds, until they crackle and smell fragrant.

Add the chopped tomatoes and cook for 4–5 minutes, mashing them, until soft. Add the chicken with all its marinade, turn the heat to high and stir-fry for 5 minutes. Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 15–20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the chicken is nearly tender and the masala is thick, with oil glistening at the edges.

Stir in the remaining biryani masala, the fried potatoes, the drained aloo bukhara and the green chillies. Cover and cook for 5 minutes more. Taste: the masala should be boldly salty and spicy, because the rice will absorb a lot of it.

Meanwhile, bring at least 3 litres of water to a rolling boil with the 2 tablespoons of salt. Add the drained rice and boil for 5–6 minutes, until the grains have lengthened and one pressed between your fingers breaks with a firm white core (about 70% cooked). Drain at once.

Spoon out half the chicken masala into a bowl. Spread a third of the rice over the masala left in the pot, then lay over the tomato slices with half the mint, coriander and reserved onions. Add the masala from the bowl, the rest of the herbs and onions, then the remaining rice. Drizzle the saffron milk (and the kewra water, if using) over the top in streaks.

Seal the pot with foil and press the lid on firmly. Cook on high heat for 2–3 minutes, until you hear a steady sizzle and see steam at the edges, then turn the heat to its lowest (set the pot on a flat griddle if your flame runs hot) and steam (dum) for 18–20 minutes, until the rice is fully tender and fluffy.

Leave the pot sealed off the heat for 5 minutes. Lift the layers out with a wide spoon from the side, so every plate gets rice, chicken, potato and plum. Check a thick piece near the bone: the meat should be white throughout with clear juices. Serve with raita and kachumber salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
